articles.title: Plans to Develop Wasteland Around Rochdale Train Station Confirmed
articles.excerpt: Plans to transform the wasteland surrounding Rochdale train station into a usable space have been confirmed, marking a significant step towards improving the area.
articles.content_html:
Plans to develop the wasteland around Rochdale train station have been confirmed. Local authorities aim to enhance the environment and accessibility for commuters and residents.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts to revitalise the area, which has been largely neglected in recent years. The local council stated that the project will improve aesthetic appeal and provide additional facilities for the community.

Specific details regarding the timeline and nature of the developments are yet to be announced. Stakeholders are optimistic that this project will lead to increased foot traffic and economic activity in the vicinity of the station.

Residents and commuters are encouraged to monitor the progress of this project, as it is expected to positively impact local transport and community engagement.

articles.title: Office of Rail and Road Rejects Proposal for Extra Rochdale to London Train Services
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has turned down a proposal for additional train services from Rochdale to London, citing concerns over delays and capacity on the West Coast Main Line.
articles.content_html:
Plans to enhance the rail link between Rochdale and London have been rejected once again. The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) announced that it had turned down proposals from Lumo to operate up to four additional return services from Rochdale to Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three services on Sundays.

Rochdale MP Paul Waugh had supported the bid, describing it as a "game-changing opportunity" for the borough and the wider North West. However, the ORR's assessment concluded that adding more trains to the already congested West Coast Main Line would likely lead to increased delays and cancellations for passengers. This decision follows a similar rejection of Lumo's application last year, with the ORR stating that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the line had not materially changed since then.

An external review commissioned by the ORR corroborated these findings, indicating that the current timetable must allow for recovery time during disruptions to minimise delays. The ORR emphasised the importance of maintaining service reliability for existing passengers.

The rejection of this proposal means that residents of Rochdale will not see an increase in direct train services to London in the near future, which could impact travel options for commuters and those wishing to visit the capital.

articles.title: Lifts at Freehold Tram Stop Out of Service Until Further Notice
articles.excerpt: The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are currently out of service due to replacement works, affecting journeys towards Manchester and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
The lifts at Freehold Tram Stop are out of service as of 6:59pm on Sunday, 18 October 2026, due to ongoing lift replacement works. This affects both platforms, with the lift towards Manchester and the lift towards Rochdale currently unavailable.

Passengers are advised to alight at either South Chadderton or Westwood tram stops and use the orange call point located at all stops to request assistance for completing their journeys. For further assistance, customers can contact the helpline at 0161 244 1000, which operates from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

The duration of the lift outage is currently unspecified, and no further updates have been provided regarding when the service will resume. Passengers are encouraged to plan their journeys accordingly and allow extra time for travel.

Transport for Greater Manchester apologises for any inconvenience caused by this disruption and is working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
articles.excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
articles.content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

Would your family use a pump track in Castleton, and what would you like a future design to include? Share your views in the comments.

articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Wednesday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

The council confirms the Rochdale display is on Wednesday 4 November 2026: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/481/rochdale-bonfire-and-fireworks-display

articles.title: Simister and Bowlee’s cross-border plan includes 200 homes in Rochdale, not 1,550
articles.excerpt: Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.
articles.content_html:
Simister and Bowlee’s housing programme crosses the borough boundary. Bury Council identifies 1,550 homes overall, of which 200 would be in Rochdale. Only the Rochdale share belongs in a total of this borough’s new housing.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

articles.title: Rochdale October half-term 2026: school dates and free family activities
articles.excerpt: The council's recommended half-term runs from 26 to 30 October. Here are verified free activities at Rochdale Town Hall, Wardle Library and local family hubs, plus what parents should check before travelling.
articles.content_html:
Families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow can start planning the October school break, with the council recommending Monday 26 to Friday 30 October 2026 as the autumn half-term holiday. The dates are a borough-wide recommended pattern, rather than a guarantee for every school, so parents should check their own school's calendar before booking childcare or a trip.

One of the clearest free options announced so far is at Rochdale Town Hall. Its Spooktacular Half Term programme is advertised for every day from Monday 26 October to Sunday 1 November, running from 10am to 4pm at the Town Hall on The Esplanade, OL16 1AZ. The organiser describes family-friendly Halloween activities, with free entry and no advance booking required. More detailed individual activities have not yet all been listed, so it is worth checking the official Town Hall event information before travelling.

For families wanting a short outing at the end of the break, Wardle Library's Kids' Club is listed in the council's October events calendar for Saturday 31 October. The free session runs from 10am until 12.30pm at 448 Birch Road, Wardle, OL12 9LH. It is aimed at families with children aged four and over and normally includes crafts, activities and challenges. The council says there is no need to book.

Parents and carers with younger children also have the borough's family hubs to investigate. Council information lists activities for children aged up to five at locations including Heybrook, Howard Street, Meanwood, Castleton, Deeplish and Sandbrook, as well as centres in Middleton, Heywood, Littleborough and the wider Pennines area. The council describes these activities as free unless otherwise stated. The listing is a directory rather than a confirmed half-term timetable, so families should consult their nearest hub's current programme instead of assuming ordinary weekly sessions continue during the holiday.

Not every regular children's library session runs during school holidays. Some Bookstart activities are explicitly described as term-time sessions, making it especially important to check dates rather than turn up on the strength of a weekly listing.

Parents trying to keep costs down can therefore rely on the confirmed free Town Hall programme and check the Wardle Library listing, while using the council's event directory to see whether anything else is added nearer the time. This guide covers confirmed information available on 13 October; opening arrangements and individual sessions may change.

Useful official sources: Rochdale Borough Council's 2026–27 school holiday calendar; the council's Spooktacular Half Term at Rochdale Town Hall listing; the council's libraries events calendar and Wardle Kids' Club entry; and the council's Family Hub Activities directory. Verify any last-minute change with the organiser before setting off.

Passengers are advised to plan their journeys ahead of time and can contact the Metrolink customer service for assistance, especially as the lift at Besses o' th' Barn tram stop is out of service. articles.title: Rochdale-London Train Service Proposal Rejected by Regulator
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has rejected plans for a direct train service between Rochdale and London Euston, disappointing local MP Paul Waugh and rail operator Lumo.
articles.content_html:
The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) has rejected a proposal for a new train service between Rochdale and London Euston, which aimed to provide four daily return services. The decision has been met with disappointment from Rochdale's MP Paul Waugh and the rail operator Lumo, who had hoped to launch the service by 2028.

The ORR stated that the additional services could increase the risk of delays spreading across the network, ultimately worsening reliability for all passengers. In a statement, Paul Waugh expressed his deep disappointment, highlighting the significance of the service for residents in Rochdale and the surrounding borough. He remains committed to improving transport connections with both Manchester and London.

Waugh noted that there are still reasons for optimism regarding future rail developments. He mentioned the Bee Network, which is set to enhance local rail services across Greater Manchester starting in 2028, and the government's ongoing efforts with Northern Powerhouse Rail, which aims to improve capacity on the West Coast Main Line.

The ORR also rejected similar applications from Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company for Wrexham-London services and Avanti West Coast for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for Lumo indicated that they are considering their next steps following the ORR's decision.

The idea to have four daily return services between Rochdale and London was rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The reason given was that the additional services could ‘increase the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers’. Low-cost rail operator Lumo had hoped to start services by 2028, with the plans receiving the backing of Rochdale MP Paul Waugh. Both shared their disappointment following the announcement. Paul Waugh, Rochdale’s MP, said: “I am deeply disappointed that the ORR has rejected the proposal for a direct Rochdale to London service. I know how much this would have meant to people in Rochdale and the wider borough, and I remain committed to improving our connections with both Manchester and London. “There are reasons to be hopeful about the future. The Bee Network is bringing greater integration of local rail services across Greater Manchester from 2028 onwards, while the government is progressing Northern Powerhouse Rail and has set out its long-term intention to develop a new rail connection between Birmingham and Manchester to increase capacity on the West Coast Main Line. “These are important investments in our rail network, and I will continue to make the case for Rochdale to benefit from better and more reliable transport links, including to London.” The ORR explained that gaps in the current timetable provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. The government body concluded that adding more services into these windows would reduce that resilience and increase risk of disruption. The ORR also rejected the application of Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR) for four return Wrexham-London Euston services and Avanti West Coast’s application for additional Blackpool-Euston services. A spokesperson for FirstGroup, who run the Lumo operation, said: “We are disappointed that the ORR has declined our revised application for new Lumo services between London and Rochdale, and we are considering our next steps. “Following the initial decision, we amended our plans in line with feedback and believe the revised proposal demonstrated strong economic benefits for passengers and communities. “It would have delivered the benefits of competition, including greater choice, lower fares and new opportunities for growth across Manchester and the north west. “Open access services have an important role to play in improving connectivity, attracting more people to rail and supporting economic development, all at no cost to the public purse. “We remain convinced that this route offered a compelling case for investment and long-term benefits for communities, businesses and the wider regional economy.” ORR has approved access for Avanti’s weekday 19:29 Chester to Euston service to carry passengers until December 2030. This train already runs as a fully crewed empty service so does not add another train to the route, but will benefit passengers, says the ORR. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: Bev Craig and Rochdale: will Greater Manchester's new mayor deliver beyond the city centre?
articles.excerpt: A detailed examination of Mayor Bev Craig's council voting record, Rochdale's deprivation and earnings, affordable housing and transport pledges, and the financial risks behind Greater Manchester's investment plans.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig's election as Mayor of Greater Manchester leaves Rochdale with a familiar question: will economic growth across the city-region translate into better-paid jobs, more affordable housing and better transport in the boroughs outside Manchester city centre?

Craig, the former leader of Manchester City Council, succeeded Andy Burnham after the mayoral election on 30 July 2026. The official result gave her 309,525 first- and second-preference votes, on a Greater Manchester turnout of 25.14%. Turnout in Rochdale was 22.95%, and she received 15,927 first-preference votes in the borough.

Her pledges on housing, public transport, high streets and industrial regeneration speak directly to several of Rochdale's needs. But the financial distinction between projects approved, investment proposed and outcomes delivered is essential.

ROCHDALE'S DEEPER ECONOMIC PROBLEMS

ONS figures reported through Nomis put Rochdale's employment rate for people aged 16–64 at 67.1% in the year to March 2026, against 75.5% across Great Britain. Estimated unemployment was 7.2%, compared with 4.5% nationally, although the ONS warns that survey-based local unemployment estimates have small-sample limitations.

In 2025, around 33.5% of working-age residents held a qualification at RQF Level 4 or above, compared with 48.6% nationally. The median weekly earnings of full-time employees resident in Rochdale were £689.50, against £766.60 in Great Britain.

According to the Government's 2025 English Indices of Deprivation, Rochdale's employment deprivation measure was 20.3%, among the highest of England's local authorities. A neighbourhood identified as Rochdale 010C has repeatedly appeared among the country's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods.

These figures expose the limitations of equating economic development with prosperity for existing residents. A growing regional economy does not automatically lift household earnings if local people cannot reach the jobs, lack relevant qualifications or cannot afford the homes built nearby.

A MAYOR WITHOUT A PARLIAMENTARY VOTING RECORD

Craig has never served as a Member of Parliament. Burnham was previously the MP for Leigh and a Cabinet minister. Tony Lloyd, the interim Greater Manchester mayor before Burnham, was also an MP.

Craig entered Manchester City Council in 2011 and became its leader in December 2021. Her record must therefore be examined through council and combined-authority decisions, rather than voting divisions or questions in the House of Commons. Attributing parliamentary votes to her would be incorrect.

This distinction is not unusual among English regional mayors. West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, North East Mayor Kim McGuinness and South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard had not served as MPs before taking office. The question is what experience of budgets, national negotiations and local delivery each officeholder brings, not whether a Commons career is a qualification for office.

WHAT HER COUNCIL DECISIONS SHOW

While Craig led Manchester City Council, the authority approved a 2026/27 revenue budget exceeding £1 billion and a 4.99% council tax increase, incorporating a 2% adult social care element. The council said this supported existing services, investment in communities, housing and public provision.

At the Greater Manchester Combined Authority meeting on 13 February 2026, the authority endorsed a Band D mayoral general precept of £153.95: £92.20 relating to fire and rescue and £61.75 to other mayoral functions. The decision followed a named unanimous vote. Compared with the previous year, the Band D precept rose £25.

These decisions were collective, and the latter was a proposal originally brought by Burnham, not a unilateral Craig tax policy. Nevertheless, the record is relevant when evaluating promises to reduce household costs and decisions about how services are paid for.

Craig was also a portfolio lead on the Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund and integrated investment pipeline approved in November 2025. The authority reported initial potential investment capacity in excess of £1 billion and approved borrowing of up to £150 million against future retained business rates.

The phrase '£1 billion investment' should not be mistaken for £1 billion in unencumbered grants. Parts of the programme involve repayable finance, borrowing or contributions from other institutions. How much is ultimately invested, and where, is more meaningful than the initial headline figure.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING: WHAT DOES THE PROMISE MEAN FOR ROCHDALE?

Craig has pledged 50,000 council, social and genuinely affordable homes across Greater Manchester by 2039, including 10,000 homes delivered, under construction or in the pipeline by May 2028.

The three categories in that near-term target are not equivalent. A completed home can be occupied. A home under construction may still face delivery risks. A home in the pipeline may lack full financing or planning approval.

Over roughly 13 years, 50,000 homes implies an average of nearly 3,850 annually across the region, although actual delivery is unlikely to be evenly spread. The programme relies on public and private land, delivery partners and capital funding that will vary from scheme to scheme.

Rochdale needs published borough-specific targets, a social-rent breakdown, site-by-site funding and delivery dates. 'Affordable' as a statutory housing designation is not always affordable for a household on below-average wages.

TRANSPORT: AN AREA WHERE THE MAYOR HAS DIRECT SPENDING CHOICES

Burnham's transport legacy includes the Bee Network and bringing local buses under public control. Craig has committed to extending free Bee Network bus travel to young people aged 11–16, building on the existing scheme for those aged 16–18.

Transport for Greater Manchester estimates that nearly 200,000 young people could benefit, saving families up to about £500 per eligible child a year. The proposed start date is January 2027, but detailed eligibility and the formal decision process have yet to be completed. The combined authority's forward plan lists a relevant decision for November 2026.

There is a financial trade-off: cheaper travel can widen access to education and employment, while recurring concessions can create continuing expenditure or foregone fare income. An annual programme budget, estimates of extra journeys and bus capacity would make the policy's cost clearer.

Meanwhile, Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton have longstanding demands for stronger rail and tram links. Early development funding for the Oldham–Rochdale–Heywood–Bury tram-train concept should not be confused with an approved construction budget.

In a September 2026 parliamentary answer to Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell, the Department for Transport confirmed that Greater Manchester is due £2.5 billion in Transport for City Regions funding between 2027/28 and 2031/32, and that scheme prioritisation rests with the mayor. That does not mean all of the money is free for the tram proposal: other regional transport commitments compete for the same settlement.

MIDDLETON AND ATOM VALLEY

Middleton is a practical test of whether investment can extend beyond Manchester's commercial centre.

On 25 September 2026, the GMCA approved the proposed designation of a Middleton mayoral development area, subject to the borough council's consent. Rochdale Council Cabinet endorsed the plans on 29 September. The proposed Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is intended to coordinate land, investment and regeneration.

A development corporation can help assemble and develop sites, but the designation alone creates neither jobs nor homes. Residents will need to know the initial public expenditure, which businesses are being attracted and whether vacant premises are being brought into productive use.

Atom Valley and plans for a Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre offer the possibility of advanced manufacturing employment in Rochdale. Earlier GMCA proposals included an indicative allocation of up to £15 million for the centre. Indicative funding, however, is not evidence that the whole scheme has been built or that local recruitment benefits have been achieved.

Craig's proposed £20 million Good Growth High Streets Fund raises a similar question. Although a simple division across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs would imply £2 million each, that is not the fund's published allocation mechanism. The official forward plan schedules the launch decision for 13 November 2026. Its distribution and final conditions remain important.

IS THE ECONOMIC PROGRAMME FINANCIALLY FEASIBLE?

Three kinds of promise require different financial tests: ongoing services, one-off capital construction and investment meant to generate repayments or returns.

Transport concessions may need continuing annual support. Housing and infrastructure require capital, planning approvals, land and delivery partners. Investment financed by borrowing must produce enough income or wider economic benefit to justify financing costs and risk.

The Good Growth Fund's capacity incorporates future retained business-rates income and borrowing, so its published performance should be judged against debt-service costs, reserves, expected returns and delays. Lower-than-expected project returns could restrict later investment capacity.

There is an economic case for public intervention where contaminated land, weak connectivity or low private returns prevent development. Equally, a funding announcement does not remove the possibility of construction inflation, overruns or weak returns.

None of these observations establishes that Craig's programme is either fully financed or unaffordable. An authoritative judgement requires programme-level budgets that separate committed grants from lending, approved borrowing from available cash, and announced schemes from projects ready to proceed.

HOW OTHER REGIONS ARE APPROACHING THE SAME QUESTIONS

The West Midlands, with a broadly comparable metropolitan scale, has pursued a mix of housing, regeneration and transport investment under Richard Parker. Its announced Futures Fund draws on several funding and investment partners rather than operating simply as a direct grant pot.

In Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram has pursued bus franchising and integrated transport, while South Yorkshire's Oliver Coppard has combined transport reform with access to skills and work. Their regions differ in population, devolved powers, infrastructure and financial structure, making simplistic headline spending comparisons unreliable.

For Greater Manchester, much of the institutional machinery was developed under Burnham: bus franchising, devolved transport decisions, investment coordination and city-region policy-making. Craig inherits that machinery rather than beginning from scratch.

WHAT THE BOROUGH SHOULD BE ABLE TO MEASURE

Rochdale residents should be able to see investment figures broken down by borough and funding type; affordable homes completed and their rents; local recruitment and wages on public-backed schemes; transport projects with approved construction budgets; and the proportion of high-street funding that actually reaches each community.

The same applies to Atom Valley and Middleton. How many genuinely new posts are created? How many go to Rochdale residents? How much public borrowing is involved? Which sites have actually begun construction?

Craig has made commitments that address recognisable challenges in Rochdale. Some draw on programmes already in progress; others remain targets or proposals requiring further approval. The economically meaningful comparison with Burnham and mayors elsewhere will be based on achieved outcomes and published finances, not the number of projects announced.

For Rochdale, the fundamental test is whether city-region investment reaches households facing lower wages, weaker employment prospects and inadequate transport connections — and whether the financial costs of delivering it remain transparent.

articles.excerpt: Advertisement feature: Rochdale Martial Arts Academy runs judo and Brazilian jiu jitsu classes for children and adults, from complete beginners to competitors.
articles.content_html:
This is a paid-for advertisement feature.

Rochdale Martial Arts Academy teaches judo and Brazilian jiu jitsu to children and adults.

Its children's classes take pupils from complete beginners through to competition level, and the academy says they are designed to build technique, discipline and confidence.

Adult classes are open to all levels. The academy says no previous experience, particular fitness level or equipment is needed to start, and that members can train at their own pace.

For those who want to compete, it runs sessions covering grip fighting, transitions, match conditioning and sparring.

The academy offers a free first class. Its timetable and membership options are on its website, which does not give prices or a street address in text, so newcomers should ring or email first.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway to host first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day at Bury Bolton Street Station on Monday 12 October.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway (ELR) is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day on Monday 12 October 2026.

The railway is looking for volunteers to help support a wide range of experiences, from luxury dining services and Rail Ale Trails to Days Out with Thomas and Santa Specials.

Volunteering opportunities cover events, catering and retail, with roles designed to suit a range of interests and experience. Volunteers could find themselves serving cream tea aboard a first-class carriage or helping to create the atmosphere for the Halloween Ghost Train.

The ELR said it will help match volunteers with roles that suit their interests and experience, with full training provided. No previous experience is needed.

Commercial Manager Lorna Kelly said: “If you’ve ever thought about volunteering at the East Lancashire Railway but felt unsure, or wondered whether you have the right experience, please come along to our Open Day. I’ll be there with some of our lovely volunteers, who can tell you what it’s really like to be part of the ELR.

“You can meet our events, catering and retail teams, hear about the roles available and ask any questions you have. Whether you’re ready to sign up or just curious, we’d love to meet you.”

The Open Day will take place at the Trackside Bar at Bury Bolton Street Station from 10am to 3pm on Monday 12 October.

The railway says prospective volunteers can attend to find out more about the roles available, meet members of the teams and ask questions before deciding whether to get involved.

Source: East Lancashire Railway.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

articles.title: No trains between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria this week as replacement buses run
articles.excerpt: Passengers travelling between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are being advised to allow extra time this week, with trains replaced by buses from Monday 10 to Friday 14 August.
articles.content_html:
Rail passengers travelling between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are facing disruption this week, with no train service operating on the route from Monday 10 August to Friday 14 August 2026 because of planned engineering work.

Rail replacement buses are operating between Manchester Victoria and Rochdale. Passengers can use a direct replacement service or a stopping service calling at Moston, Mills Hill and Castleton. Travellers making the full journey between Rochdale and Manchester Victoria are advised to use the direct replacement bus where possible.

The disruption has prompted concern locally after passengers checking journeys discovered that their usual trains had been replaced. One post in the Rochdale Borough Noticeboard Facebook group said: ‘Just noticed there are no trains from Rochdale to Manchester this week, only replacement buses.’

The closure forms part of planned engineering work affecting services into and out of Manchester Victoria. Other Calder Valley services are operating to revised timetables, so passengers travelling beyond Rochdale should check their individual journey before setting off.

Replacement buses generally take longer than the normal rail journey and passengers should leave additional time, particularly during busy commuting periods. Anyone with onward connections is advised to check the latest timetable before travelling.

The disruption is currently scheduled to continue through Friday 14 August, with passengers advised to check National Rail or their train operator for the latest journey information before setting off.

articles.title: New Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig visits Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Newly elected Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today as she begins work across the city-region following her victory in last month's mayoral by-election.
articles.content_html:
Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

At the time of publication, no detailed public itinerary or standalone press release about today's Rochdale visit had been published on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority news pages. Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

Rochdale Daily will add any confirmed detail released by the mayor's press team about the purpose of the visit, people she met or commitments made while in the borough.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

IMAGE NOTE: The historic Aerofilms photographs referenced above are held by Britain From Above. Their terms do not permit commercial reproduction without a separate licence, so Rochdale Daily links readers to the original archive images rather than reproducing them without permission.

articles.title: Rochdale's biggest event returns this Saturday as Feel Good Festival takes over the town centre
articles.excerpt: Thousands of people are expected to descend on Rochdale town centre this Saturday as the borough's biggest annual event returns with headline performances from Gabrielle, Ash and Starsailor alongside a packed programme of live music, street food and family entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest and most attended annual event returns on Saturday 8 August as the Feel Good Festival once again transforms the town centre into one of Greater Manchester's largest free celebrations of live music, food and entertainment.

Thousands of visitors are expected to flock to Rochdale throughout the day, with the stunning backdrop of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall providing the setting for a packed programme of performances, street food and family activities.

Headlining this year's main stage in Town Hall Square is BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, whose career has produced chart-topping hits including Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She will be joined by legendary Northern Irish rock band Ash and indie favourites Starsailor, alongside performances from The Allergies, Alex Spencer, K-STATE, Metro and Dave Sweetmore.

Away from the main stage, live music will continue throughout the day inside venues across Rochdale town centre, with pubs, bars and independent venues hosting local artists and emerging talent, creating a festival atmosphere across the borough.

The festival officially opens at 11:30am, with entertainment continuing throughout the afternoon and evening before the headline performances conclude at approximately 10:45pm.

One of the festival's biggest attractions remains its popular Food and Drink Village, where visitors can enjoy everything from gourmet burgers and pizzas to international street food, loaded fries, desserts, artisan coffee, ice cream, licensed bars and locally produced drinks. Independent traders from across the region will once again showcase a wide variety of food and beverages throughout the day.

Visitors travelling by car are encouraged to use Rochdale town centre's public car parks, including those at Number One Riverside, Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre and nearby council-operated facilities. Due to the popularity of the event and temporary road closures, organisers recommend arriving early or making use of public transport wherever possible. Rochdale Railway Station, Rochdale Interchange and the Bee Network Metrolink stop are all within a short walking distance of the festival site.

The event has been designed to be accessible for everyone. Step-free routes are available throughout the main festival site, accessible toilets are provided, designated accessible viewing areas will be available near the main stage and British Sign Language interpretation will accompany selected performances. Festival stewards will also be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors requiring additional support.

Since launching in 2008, the Feel Good Festival has welcomed internationally renowned artists to Rochdale and has become one of the North West's premier town-centre music festivals. Beyond the entertainment, it provides a significant boost to the local economy, with restaurants, cafés, bars, shops and hotels all benefiting from the influx of visitors.

Whether you're heading into town to sing along with Gabrielle, relive the guitar anthems of Ash, enjoy Starsailor's iconic hits or simply spend the day sampling fantastic food while supporting local businesses, the Feel Good Festival promises another unforgettable celebration of everything Rochdale has to offer.

articles.title: Taxi driver issues safety warning after frightening incident near Littleborough railway station
articles.excerpt: A taxi driver has shared details of a frightening incident near Littleborough railway station in the hope of encouraging colleagues to remain vigilant while waiting for bookings.
articles.content_html:
A taxi driver has urged colleagues across Rochdale borough to remain vigilant after describing a frightening encounter while waiting for his next booking near Littleborough railway station.

The driver said the incident happened shortly after completing an Uber journey from Rochdale Railway Station to a passenger drop-off in Littleborough. After finishing the fare, he parked on a nearby street opposite Littleborough Railway Station while waiting for his next booking.

According to the driver's account, a man described as a white British male aged between 35 and 45 approached the vehicle accompanied by a dog. The driver says the man opened the car door without permission before placing the dog inside the vehicle, along with a bag containing unknown items.

When challenged, the driver alleges the man became aggressive and attempted to damage the vehicle by striking one of the windows. Fearing for his safety, the driver immediately contacted Greater Manchester Police while remaining inside the vehicle.

The driver says the alleged aggression continued while he was speaking to police, prompting him to drive to a safer, busier location near Sainsbury's Local in Littleborough, where he waited for officers to arrive.

Police subsequently attended the scene, took a statement and dealt with the reported incident. Rochdale Daily has approached Greater Manchester Police to establish whether any arrests were made or investigations remain ongoing.

Following the incident, the driver shared his experience publicly in the hope of preventing something similar from happening to others working in the taxi trade.

He is encouraging drivers to avoid waiting for jobs in isolated streets where possible and instead use well-lit locations with passing pedestrians or nearby businesses. He also advises drivers to keep vehicle doors locked while waiting for bookings and to contact police immediately if they feel threatened.

Personal safety is an important consideration for taxi and private hire drivers, many of whom work alone at all hours of the day and night. Drivers frequently find themselves waiting for bookings in unfamiliar locations or transporting passengers they have never previously met. Industry organisations have long encouraged drivers to remain aware of their surroundings, keep communication devices readily available and report suspicious or aggressive behaviour promptly.

While incidents of this nature remain relatively uncommon, they serve as a reminder of the challenges faced by those working in the transport sector. For many drivers, particularly those working evening and overnight shifts, staying alert and choosing safe waiting locations forms an important part of their daily routine.

Anyone who witnesses criminal damage, threatening behaviour or any incident where someone feels at immediate risk should contact Greater Manchester Police on 999 in an emergency, or report non-emergency incidents by calling 101 or using the force's online reporting service.

articles.title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Reform's strongest showing yet reshapes Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Labour retained the Greater Manchester mayoralty, but Reform UK's strongest regional performance to date has reshaped the political landscape and established the party as the city's principal opposition force.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester has elected a new mayor, with Labour's Bev Craig succeeding Andy Burnham after winning the mayoral by-election. While Labour retained the office, one of the election's defining stories was the emergence of Reform UK as the city's principal opposition force, with Sian Astley delivering the party's strongest performance in a Greater Manchester-wide contest to date.

Craig secured 309,525 votes in the final round, representing 66.3 per cent of the vote, while Reform UK's Sian Astley received 157,178 votes, or 33.7 per cent. The result followed a second-round count after no candidate achieved an outright majority of first-preference votes.

Astley's campaign marked a significant moment for Reform UK in Greater Manchester. Standing on a platform centred on neighbourhood policing, transparency in regional government, public spending and directing more investment towards towns across all ten boroughs, she introduced the party's message to hundreds of thousands of voters and established Reform as Labour's most significant electoral challenger in the city-region.

The first-preference vote illustrated that shift. Astley secured 111,928 votes, comfortably finishing ahead of every other opposition candidate. While Labour maintained its lead, Reform's result demonstrated that many voters are now looking beyond the traditional political parties, reflecting wider political changes seen across England over recent years.

The election also highlighted the scale of the challenge facing every political party in reconnecting with the electorate. Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the Greater Manchester mayoralty was introduced in 2017. More than three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot despite the mayor holding responsibility for transport, policing, housing, regeneration, adult education funding and significant economic investment across the region.

For many observers, that figure raises important questions about public engagement with devolved government. The office of Mayor of Greater Manchester has become one of the most influential elected positions outside Westminster, yet millions of residents continue to feel disconnected from regional politics. Whether the low turnout reflected election fatigue, limited awareness of the mayor's powers or wider political dissatisfaction will no doubt be debated in the months ahead.

Astley's campaign also carried wider historical significance. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to serve as the directly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since the office was created in 2017. Although that milestone was not reached, her candidacy demonstrated the increasing diversity of those seeking senior political office within the city-region.

The campaign itself was notable for the issues it placed at the centre of debate. Reform UK argued for greater scrutiny of Combined Authority spending, more visible neighbourhood policing, improved road maintenance and stronger accountability within regional government. Labour focused on continuing the Bee Network, delivering new housing and building on the devolution settlement developed under Andy Burnham. Voters were therefore presented with two distinctly different visions for Greater Manchester's future.

For Rochdale residents, the outcome will have practical consequences regardless of political preference. The mayor oversees Greater Manchester Police through the Police and Crime Commissioner powers, shapes strategic transport investment including the Bee Network, influences regeneration funding and represents the region in negotiations with central government. Decisions taken over the next four years will directly affect communities throughout Rochdale borough.

Although Labour retains control of the mayoralty, the election demonstrated that Greater Manchester's political landscape is becoming increasingly competitive. Reform UK's performance suggests future elections may no longer be defined by a straightforward Labour contest, with Astley's campaign establishing the party as a credible challenger across much of the city-region.

Attention now turns from campaigning to governing. Bev Craig inherits responsibility for one of England's largest devolved administrations at a time of financial pressure, growing demands on public services and continuing debate over transport, policing and housing. At the same time, Reform UK leaves the campaign with increased visibility, a larger regional profile and the opportunity to build on its strongest Greater Manchester result to date ahead of future elections.

articles.title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
articles.excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.

articles.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
articles.excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.
